Three lions die in zoo as Japan battles extreme heat
Three female lions at a Tokyo zoo have died of suspected heat-related illness, as Japan battles punishing summer temperatures.
The three lions died within a week at the Tama Zoological Park in western Tokyo. Autopsies show that the lions, aged three to 15, had suffered from dehydration and multiple organ failure - suggesting heat was the cause, said the zoo.
"This is the first time we've experienced anything like this. Last year was also hot, but none of our lions fell ill like this," Miwa, Kosaka, a zoo representative, told the BBC.
According to Tama Zoo, Mugi, a three-year-old female lion, had a loss of appetite on 19 July and was unable to stand up the next day.
Zoo staff provided ventilation and water to cool her down, and later administered subcutaneous fluids, liver tonics and vitamins. But she ultimately died on 28 July.
Ichigo, an 11-year-old female lion, died days later on 31 July. Luena, a 15-year-old female lion, died on Sunday.
Autopsies show systemic dehydration and multiple organ failure in all three lions, suggesting that heat stress was a cause, the zoo said. It added that their causes of death can only be determined after test results are out.
There are three lions - two males and one female - that are "still unwell and unable to stand", the zoo said in a statement on Monday, adding that its staff are administering fluids, medication and vitamins to the big cats.
"Some of the lions are showing signs of improvement," Kosaka told the BBC.
Four lions had shown signs of recovery, the zoo said, while six had been in good health from the beginning. They will be placed in a private enclosure equipped with portable air-conditioners and industrial fans.
Hideaki Karaki, professor of veterinary medicine at the University of Tokyo, told local media that high humidity makes it difficult for lions to regulate their body temperatures.
He explains that instead of sweating, lions take deep breaths to expel moisture from their airways. When the moisture evaporates, body temperature drops.
But the lions' body temperatures could not drop sufficiently in high humidity, he says.
Another factor could be the sudden spike in temperature in mid-July, leaving the animals insufficient time to acclimatise to the heat, Karaki adds.
Tama Zoo houses about 260 species of animals. Its lions have long been a key attraction, having been bred and exhibited since 1964. According to the zoo's website, it offers a safari-style bus service for visitors to view the lions in their enclosure.
Tama Zoo announced last month that it would suspend its lion exhibit and lion bus service, due to the "sudden heatwave" making the lions ill.
More than 43,000 people across Japan have been taken into hospital for heatstroke in this summer alone.
Additional reporting by Chie Kobayashi

Customers browse summer selections in an Olive Young store in Jongno District, central Seoul, on July 31.LIM SUN-YOUNG
Cool has never been hotter. Korea's record-breaking heat wave is reshaping consumer habits, as shoppers look beyond handheld fans and iced drinks to products that help them feel cooler throughout the day.
"These days, if it doesn't keep you cool, it doesn't sell," an industry source said on Sunday. "Cooling products have become must-have items for consumers and a necessity for businesses."
A dedicated "Survival Beauty" section at a CJ Olive Young store in Jongno District, central Seoul, brought together products designed to combat extreme heat, such as cooling sunscreens, skincare for irritated skin, oil- and sweat-control products and cooling treatment on Friday.
"I always use a setting spray so my makeup doesn't melt from sweat," one shopper at the store said.
"These days, I regularly use cooling face creams and face masks to lower my skin temperature," another shopper added.
Sales of makeup setting sprays jumped 864 percent between July 1 and July 29 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to CJ Olive Young. During the same period, searches on the retailer's online mall for cooling oil-control products and "cooling spray" surged 1,870 percent and 160 percent, respectively.
"Foundation-free" makeup, which minimizes the use of foundation, and "sun layering," the practice of reapplying sunscreen throughout the day, have emerged as two of this summer's biggest beauty trends.
The prolonged heat is even changing men's grooming habits. Sales of facial cleanser products rose 280 percent from July 4 to 10 compared with the same period a month earlier, according to 4910, a men's beauty and fashion platform.
The scorching weather is also driving demand for K-beauty products overseas.
Korean sunscreens, which are already popular abroad, are seeing sales spikes in Britain, according to Pureseoul, a K-beauty retailer in the United Kingdom.
Korean cosmetics original development manufacturers Kolmar Korea and Cosmax are expected to post record quarterly earnings for the second quarter of 2026, supported by growing exports of sun care products.
Cooling technology is reshaping wardrobes as well.
Functional cooling features have become a key selling point as fashion and outdoor brands expand cooling technology beyond T-shirts to shirts, pants, skirts, innerwear and even shoes.
Searches for "cooling" products on fashion platform Musinsa increased 68 percent in June from a year earlier, while sales of cooling innerwear at Daiso rose 40 percent over the same period.
Workwear is also getting a cooling upgrade. One of the latest innovations is fan-equipped workwear that circulates air inside the garment to lower the wearer's apparent temperature.
Cooling bedding and towels are also flying off shelves. Sales of cooling bedding at lifestyle brand Casamia increased 2.5 times in June from the previous month, while sales of cooling towels from Kleannara rose 323 percent compared with a year earlier.
"As climate change becomes part of everyday life, consumers will continue seeking functional products that do more than simply help them escape the heat," said Lee Eun-hee, professor of consumer studies at Inha University. "They will increasingly look for products that actively lower apparent temperatures."
BY LIM SUN-YOUNG [lee.jiwon10@joongang.co.kr]

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday directed authorities to step up support for people affected by a record-breaking heatwave after the death toll from heat-related causes rose to 16.
Speaking at a cabinet meeting, Lee called for urgent measures to protect vulnerable residents, ensure the stability of the power grid as air-conditioner use surges, and overhaul the country's disaster response system, warning that extreme weather is becoming increasingly frequent rather than exceptional.
"We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system, since this extreme weather is becoming normal," Lee said.
South Korea's weather agency said the southeastern inland city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5°C (108.5°F) on Sunday, the highest officially recorded in the country's 122 years of weather observations.
The Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) also issued its first-ever severe heatwave warning for parts of Seoul and neighbouring Gyeonggi Province on Monday before expanding it to cover the entire capital on Tuesday, underscoring the exceptional nature of the ongoing heatwave.
Why is this heatwave unusual?While South Korea typically experiences hot and humid summers under the influence of the East Asian monsoon, temperatures above 40°C are exceptionally rare. The country has a temperate climate with four distinct seasons, and average daytime temperatures during July and August generally range between 25°C and 30°C. The extreme heat also reflects a broader shift in the country's climate patterns.
According to the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA), the current heatwave is being driven by a combination of meteorological and climate factors. A key reason is the earlier expansion and prolonged influence of the North Pacific high-pressure system, which is allowing hot and humid air to persist over the Korean Peninsula for longer than usual.
Strong summer sunshine further intensifies daytime heating, while warmer surrounding sea surface temperatures help maintain high humidity and keep overnight temperatures elevated, resulting in more frequent tropical nights.
According to the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA), South Korea's heatwaves are becoming more frequent, arriving earlier in the year and lasting longer than they did in the past. The agency's analysis found that the country has experienced significantly more heatwave days and tropical nights over the past decade than in previous decades, reflecting a clear shift towards more prolonged and intense summer heat.

Three lions from a Tokyo zoo have died from suspected heatstroke and others are undergoing treatment, a spokesperson said on Tuesday, as the big cats struggle in Japan’s high levels of humidity.
Japan sweltered through its hottest summer on record last year and parts of the country have hit 40C in recent weeks, qualifying for the new “cruelly hot day” designation.
Since mid-July, 10 of the 16 lions in Tama zoological park have suffered from “loss of appetite and decreased activity”, and three lionesses had died, the zoo said in a statement. One lioness died on Tuesday, another Friday, and the third on Sunday, it said.
The cause of the deaths is suspected to be heatstroke, as dehydration and multiple organ failure were observed by a veterinarian, the zoo said.
“Even though lions are thought to be resistant to heat, zoo keepers have been strengthening countermeasures to cope with Japan’s summer heat in recent years. Heat here comes with high humidity; that is different from heat with dry air in Africa,” a zoo spokesperson said.
“But this summer, heat arrived suddenly after the rainy season was over” in late July, they added.
“We are strengthening measures against the heat, sprinkling water, improving ventilation and installing spot air conditioners.”
The zoo said several lions are still being treated.
About 18,600 people in Japan were taken to hospital for heatstroke between 20 and 26 July, with 45 of them pronounced dead on arrival, according to the fire and disaster management agency.
Authorities have adjusted the timings of a string of cultural and sporting events in recent years because of the heat, including the World Cosplay Summit in Nagoya, which held its last summer edition last weekend.
Japan experiences about 1,300 heat-related deaths annually and is aiming to halve that number by 2030. The country’s highest recorded temperature was registered in August last year: 41.8C in Isesaki, north of Tokyo.
Scientists say human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events in Japan and elsewhere. South Korea is currently engulfed by a heatwave, with the rising summer temperatures linked to at least 16 deaths.

A truck sprays water to cool down a road in central Seoul on Aug. 4.YONHAP
Outdoor construction works and events were suspended in Seoul on Tuesday as an emergency heat wave warning was issued across the entire city.
The Korea Meteorological Administration placed the city under effect at 11 a.m.
The emergency heat wave warning, the highest level of three-tier heat alert, is issued when the apparent temperature is forecast to reach at least 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit) or the mercury is expected to hit 39 degrees Celsius or higher.
The Seoul Metropolitan Government immediately suspended outdoor work at all 56 construction sites commissioned by the city. It also instructed private construction companies to adopt the same protective measures. The city plans to inspect individual worksites to ensure compliance.
Older adults’ outdoor labor under the city's senior employment programs was also suspended. Only limited indoor duties in air-conditioned facilities will be permitted. Park workers will also be instructed to stop outdoor work.
The city also canceled outdoor cultural, tourism and youth events.
Five outdoor programs scheduled between Tuesday and Sunday were canceled, including musical performances on the lawn in front of City Hall and a guided excursion program that follows the Hanyang Doseong, which is known as the historic Seoul city wall.
The city will also suspend cultural tourism interpretation services at major tourist attractions. Its roving tourist information service across eight tourist areas — includingthe neighborhoods of Myeongdong, Bukchon and Namdaemun — has also been temporarily suspended.
The city will also intensify road cooling operations. Street washing, previously carried out three to four times a day, will increase to as many as six times daily under the emergency heat wave warning.
Additional privately operated water trucks will be deployed to spray roads in the city center and along major thoroughfares. District offices will receive extra disaster management funding from the city government to expand their own water truck operations.
The Seoul city government has also provided 440 million won ($307,500) in emergency special adjustment grants to help its 25 district offices respond to the heat wave.
In addition, the city will provide 40,000 won in cooling subsidies to about 410,000 low-income households. It will also cover two months of air conditioning costs for short-term residential facilities and welfare centers for people with disabilities. The city will finance the 20.5 billion won needed for the measures through its disaster relief fund.
The city will maintain its emergency heat wave response system until the heat wave alert is lifted.
“Extreme heat is no longer a temporary inconvenience,” Seoul Mayor Oh Se-hoon said. “It is a disaster that threatens the lives and health of Seoulites. We will pay even closer attention to vulnerable residents while ensuring the safety of everyone working in the field.”

Top-level heat wave warning expands across Seoul amid life-threatening temperatures
Seoul and parts of Gyeonggi will see the mercury exceed 39 degrees Celsius (102.2 degrees Fahrenheit) as authorities urge people to avoid outdoor activity.
Heat haze rises from an asphalt road in western Seoul's Yeouido district on Aug. 3 as heat wave advisories remain in effect across most of the country.NEWS1
A top-level heat wave emergency warning was expanded Tuesday to cover all of Seoul and parts of northern Gyeonggi, as temperatures in the greater Seoul area are forecast to exceed 39 degrees Celsius (102.2 degrees Fahrenheit).
“Easterly winds are expected to continue flowing into the greater Seoul area for the time being, driving temperatures significantly higher,” the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said. “Highs are expected to exceed 39 degrees Celsius in Seoul and parts of Gyeonggi, bringing life-threatening extreme heat.”
The KMA expanded the extreme heat emergency warning to northern Seoul on Tuesday after issuing it for the southern part of the capital the previous day. The warning, which took effect at 11 a.m., is the highest level of Korea's heat wave alert system and was introduced for the first time this year.
The warning was also issued for Goyang, Osan, Hanam, Anseong, southern Paju, northern Yongin and the southeastern and western parts of Yeoju in Gyeonggi. Daytime temperatures in those areas are expected to reach as high as 39 degrees Celsius, with some locations potentially exceeding 40 degrees Celsius.
“All nonessential outdoor activities and outdoor work should be suspended or postponed as much as possible,” KMA said. “People should move to cool places such as shaded areas, heat shelters or air-conditioned facilities, and stay hydrated and get adequate rest.”
Extreme heat is also expected to continue across the southern regions, including the Honam region, where the highest-level heat wave warning remains in effect. Honam refers to Gwangju and the Jeolla region.
Showers are forecast from the afternoon into the evening in southern Gyeonggi, the Chungcheong and Jeolla regions, inland western Gyeongsang and the mountainous areas of Jeju Island. Temperatures may temporarily fall during the rain, but high humidity after the showers is expected to make conditions feel even hotter.
The KMA said the extreme heat is likely to persist as clear weather continues for the time being.
One variable is Typhoon Dolphin, the season's 13th named storm, which is approaching the Korean Peninsula.
As of 9 a.m. Tuesday, Dolphin was moving west at 16 kilometers per hour (9.9 miles per hour) over waters about 1,530 kilometers (950 miles) east of Okinawa, Japan. The storm had a central pressure of 950 hectopascals and maximum sustained winds of 43 meters per second (96 miles per hour), classifying it as a Category 3-strength typhoon under the KMA's five-tier intensity scale.
Dolphin is expected to pass Okinawa on Friday as it continues moving westward. In the process, it could strengthen the heat wave by driving strong easterly winds into the Korean Peninsula.
It remains uncertain whether Dolphin will make landfall in China or turn toward Korea afterward.
“For now, there is a strong possibility that Dolphin will affect waters off Jeju and become a typhoon that impacts Korea,” Kang Nam-young, a geography professor at Kyungpook National University, said. “Whether its track opens a path for it to affect inland areas is something we need to watch more closely.”

This extreme reading marks the fifth consecutive day temperatures have exceeded 40 degrees Celsius in the region, intensifying a heatwave that has prompted heightened alerts throughout the country. In addition to Yangsan, other cities including Daegu and Busan have also experienced high temperatures, with many areas climbing into the upper 30s. Authorities are urging residents to stop all outdoor activities immediately in these regions. Indoor spaces lacking air conditioning have been classified as 'dangerous,' further compelling individuals to seek shelter in air-conditioned venues such as shopping malls and cafés. Ju Dong-yeol, a 27-year-old office worker, described his experience in a Starbucks in South Korea’s capital, saying, "it is too hot to be outside doing anything." He added, "I can’t think of anything else to do other than stay in air-conditioned places like home, shopping malls and cafés." The city of Gyeongju, located approximately 240 kilometres south-east of Seoul, recorded a high of 40.3 degrees Celsius on Sunday, its highest in eight years. The oppressive heat is also being felt across the border in North Korea, where state media reported temperatures reaching 40 degrees Celsius in certain regions. Residents in Pyongyang have endured nights with temperatures not dropping below 25 degrees Celsius over the past week. On Sunday, more than 20 areas across South Korea were placed under emergency heatwave alerts, a new warning system implemented this year to address rising temperatures. An emergency alert is triggered when forecasts predict perceived temperatures of 38 degrees Celsius or actual temperatures of 39 degrees Celsius. In issuing warnings, the KMA advised people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities” and to find refuge in designated cooling areas or shaded spaces while maintaining hydration. In light of the heatwave, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong-sook has directed local officials to enhance safety checks on vulnerable populations and ensure reliable power and water supplies. Forecasts indicate that easterly winds may drive the extreme heat further inland on Monday, with Seoul expected to reach a temperature of 37 degrees Celsius. The KMA anticipates temperatures in South Jeolla and South Gyeongsang to exceed 39 degrees Celsius, creating conditions that may pose life-threatening risks. Officials are also monitoring Typhoon Dolphin, which is presently moving towards the southeast coast of China, south of the Korean peninsula. The storm's trajectory could influence the duration of the unbearable heat. Should the typhoon steer towards eastern China, it may exacerbate humidity levels, thus intensifying the existing heatwave. Conversely, if it approaches the southern areas of the peninsula, the storm could bring stronger winds and cloud cover, providing some respite from the heat. Data from the KMA reveals that the average annual incidence of heatwave days has more than doubled to 19 in the past five years, with a heatwave day defined as one where the maximum temperature reaches at least 33 degrees Celsius. In response to the soaring temperatures, South Korea's professional baseball league cancelled a game in Changwon after the city’s temperature hit 39.5 degrees Celsius, marking the second consecutive cancellation of games in the area. The Korea Baseball Organization released a statement that prioritised the safety and health of spectators and players amid the ongoing severe heatwave warnings. Scientists have highlighted that extreme weather events such as heatwaves are becoming increasingly frequent and severe as a consequence of anthropogenic climate change. This year's return of El Niño, a natural climatic occurrence that raises Pacific Ocean surface temperatures, is also contributing to the extreme weather conditions, typically occurring every two to seven years.

SEOUL: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung urged authorities on Tuesday (Aug 4) to step up support for people affected by a record heatwave in the country, saying the death toll had risen to 16 and warning that extreme weather was becoming more frequent.
Speaking at a Cabinet meeting, Lee called on officials to take necessary measures to protect the daily lives of people and inspect power systems as demand for air conditioning surges.
"We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system, since this extreme weather is becoming normal," he said.

The heatwave impacting parts of the UK this week continues into Tuesday with a risk of thunderstorms in some parts.
Pershore in Worcestershire and Cavendish in Suffolk hit three consecutive days of heatwave threshold temperatures on Monday and it is expected more parts of southern and eastern England will reach heatwave criteria on Tuesday.
Amber and yellow heat health alerts, external are in effect across much of England until 09:00 BST Wednesday, with temperatures expected to reach more than 30C in some areas.
The intense heat will be short lived though as a change in the weather pattern is on the way from midweek.
When will the heatwave end?
During Tuesday, a cold front will move southwards across the Midlands and into south-east England. However, it is unlikely to deliver any meaningful rainfall.
Some areas in the far south-east, including London, Essex, Kent and Surrey, are unlikely to receive any rain at all.
This is a pattern that has become all too familiar in recent weeks, as the UK experienced its driest and sunniest July on record.
Areas of low pressure have tracked to the north of the UK, bringing below-average rainfall and consistently failing to deliver any meaningful rain further south.
Flash flooding and hail risk
Low pressure which has recently brought rainfall to Scotland, Northern Ireland and parts of northern England will bring scattered showers and thunderstorms on Tuesday and into Wednesday. However, this is unlikely to alleviate the current drought.
A yellow thunderstorm warning has been issued by the Met Office for parts of Northern Ireland on Tuesday.
It runs until 21:00, when up to 30mm of rain in an hour or two is possible, along with strong winds and the chance of hail.
Areas that do see a heavy downpour are at risk of flash flooding.
The scorched ground, dry grass and soil caused by the lack of rain is likely to cause significant pooling and runoff, as rainfall struggles to get absorbed during brief bursts of heavy rain.
Hail may accompany the most intense downpours which could come as a surprise following the predominantly hot and dry conditions.
Hail is most common in summer months as it needs to develop inside towering cumulonimbus clouds, which are often spawned by intense heat at ground level.
Will there be another heatwave?
Following one of the driest and hottest stretches of weather in the UK's history, the indications are that August is likely to bring more of the same.
Forecast models suggest low rainfall and above average temperatures will continue for much of the UK, meaning it is unlikely that any of the hosepipe bans affecting more than 20 million people in England and Wales will be lifted soon.
Wisley in Surrey remains the driest location in the UK, having recorded 47 consecutive days without measurable rainfall, while many other parts of the UK have had a fraction of their normal rainfall in June and July.
Further spikes of heat are likely, however as August wears on and the sun gradually loses some of its intensity, the likelihood of extreme temperatures in the high 30s lessens.
But it is not uncommon to have spells of intense heat reaching 30C or higher even into September.

The ritzy neighbourhood was made globally famous by K-pop star Psy’s 2012 hit single “Gangnam Style” – lauding the lifestyles of its ultra-rich residents.
But under million-dollar luxury apartments chilled by whirling air-conditioners, tenants in one of Seoul’s last shanty towns suffer headaches in the savage heat.
“It’s so hot that it’s hard to breathe,” said one resident of Guryong Village, a settlement of crude wood and tarpaulin shacks hosting around 160 households, according to officials.
The woman – asking to be identified by her surname, Jeong, for privacy reasons – said she could not afford to cool the one-room home shared with her husband and disabled daughter.
“The poor really suffer,” said the woman in her 60s, washing vegetables by the open door of her residence as temperatures outside soared up to 38 deg C.
South Korea is sweltering in a streak of searing weather – with new all-time highs set three times over the past week alone and temperatures peaking at 42.5 deg C on Aug 2.
Volatile weather
The capital was under a “severe heatwave warning” on Aug 4 for the first time since the new category was introduced in 2026 to alert citizens to increasing extremes.
Scientists say volatile weather events are becoming more intense and frequent owing to climate change, which is man-made.
But heatwaves are not experienced equally across the wealth divide.
In exclusive Gangnam, south of the Han River, homes near the Guryong Village sell for up to 5.4 billion won (S$4.8 million) and boast all cutting-edge modern conveniences. Tree-shaded boulevards are lined with flagship Ferrari, Lamborghini and Rolls-Royce showrooms, as well as designer boutiques and Michelin-starred restaurants.
Jeong Eun-woo, who lives in one of Gangnam’s modern high-rises, has not found this summer particularly difficult.
“I’m keeping the air-conditioning running at full blast. I drink iced coffee and wear light clothes,” said the 20-year-old.

Suspected heatstroke kills three lions at Japan zoo
Audio By Vocalize
Japan sweltered through its hottest summer on record last year and parts of the country have hit 40C in recent weeks, qualifying for the new designation "cruelly hot day".
Since mid-July, 10 of the 16 lions in Tama Zoological Park have suffered symptoms such as "loss of appetite and decreased activity", and three lionesses died, the zoo said in a statement.
One passed away on Tuesday, another died on Friday, and the third died on Sunday, it said.
"According to our veterinarian, the cause of the deaths is suspected to be heatstroke" as dehydration and multiple organ failure were observed, a spokeswoman told AFP.
"Even though lions are thought to be resistant to heat, zoo keepers have been strengthening countermeasures to cope with Japan's summer heat in recent years. Heat here comes with high humidity; that is different from heat with dry air in Africa," she said.
"But this summer, heat arrived suddenly after the rainy season was over" in late July, she said.
"We are strengthening measures against the heat (further), sprinkling water, improving ventilation and installing spot air conditioners," she said.
Several lions are still being treated, she added.
Close to 18,600 people were taken to hospital for heatstroke between July 20 and 26, with 45 of them pronounced dead on arrival, according to the fire and disaster management agency.
Japan experiences about 1,300 heat-related deaths annually and is aiming to halve that number by 2030.
Scientists say human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events in Japan and elsewhere.
Its highest recorded temperature was registered on August 5, 2025, at 41.8C in Isesaki, north of Tokyo.
Authorities have adjusted the timings of a string of cultural and sporting events in recent years because of the heat, including the World Cosplay Summit in Nagoya, which held its last summer edition last weekend.

The measure applies until further notice. It does not cover freight trains carrying goods considered essential for the national economy or for the continuity of critical supply chains.
Freight trains already moving when the restriction begins will not continue through the evening peak. They are to be held at the first suitable station where this can be done without compromising operational safety. After 22:00, the trains will be released progressively, depending on traffic conditions and instructions from traffic management centres.
The decision changes the heatwave response from internal energy management into a direct operating restriction for rail freight. MÁV Group had already introduced temporary railway energy-saving measures on 31 July, including a limit on the current consumption of electric locomotives when starting and accelerating. The same package also reduces electricity use at railway properties and facilities, including non-essential lighting and air-conditioned spaces, while keeping railway operations, traffic safety, passenger safety and critical IT and communication systems at full capacity.
For freight operators, the market impact is concentrated in the evening operating window. The restriction removes five hours of normal freight movement each day on the affected Hungarian networks, with exemptions tied to the cargo’s role in critical supply chains rather than to a specific operator or route.
